doc.title: Jackie Cain and Roy Kral interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 22, 1998

chapter: Alec Wilder and the Blue Angel
title: The Blue Angel audition and cabaret as jazz clubs closed
summary: Audition for Herb Jacoby, Bart Howard, early Andy Griffith, the Bobby Short disagreement, and the shift into cabaret.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: Alec, after that, got us an audition at the Blue Angel in New York City which was run by Max Gordon who eventually owned the Village Vanguard, and the guy’s name was Jacoby.
Herb Jacoby.
Herb Jacoby. We used to call him the East Side General DeGaulle.
Because he looked like that.
And he was pompous and well—
He just had that attitude, he just had that kind of, you know, attitude.

So we auditioned, we made it, and we were put into the showroom in the back. Bart Howard was playing piano and playing all those wonderful songs of his, and there were — people would come through like Orson Bean doing his comedy act, Andy Griffith doing his comedy act.
Before anyone knew him.
Oh I didn’t know that.
This was before anybody knew him, yeah.
He was a stand-up?
Yeah. He did a stand-up doing Shakespeare and classic stories with a sort of a southern drawl and funny angles to it. It was very good, yeah. Anyway that was—

And there were several other people. And out in the bar, after the show would be over, we would do our thing and then somebody else would do this, or comedy, whatever, a lot of things were happening. Out in the bar this wonderful, exciting piano player, Bobby Short.
Honey, I have to correct you. That isn’t true.
Well I wish you hadn’t said that.
No, I know. No actually he was out there, but not when we were working there. We went there to see him once.
Well you spoiled a good story but that’s okay.
Well he doesn’t like to let the truth get in the way of a good story. But you’re busted.
Yeah, you wait.
It wasn’t Bobby Short?
No it was Bobby Short.
Yeah we went to hear him there another time, and he’s confusing it. He thinks it was when we were there but we weren’t.
Well then you owe her one.
No, absolutely not.

He’s telling the truth, but you see at this time a lot of the jazz clubs were drying up, like 52nd Street wasn’t happening anymore, and there weren’t that many clubs. A lot of clubs were closing, and we were thinking what were we going to do next you know. And so when the opportunity came along for us to do this audition, we thought hey that’s great, that’s how we started to getting in to some cabaret, you know what they called cabaret. At that time it was just a joint, it was a saloon you know. But now it’s cabaret. And that was an elegant place and they had very good performers all the time. Just hearing all these great comedians in there, they were very funny and we enjoyed the other people working there as well as Bart Howard, and so it was a good opportunity for us. We were there about a month. And I don’t remember what happened quite after that. Do you?
